title: People can support strong environmental goals while rejecting a policy they think will raise their bills
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35073, comparing a probability-based representative U.S. sample with environmental economists and testing educational videos about pass-through and cost-effectiveness
geography: United States; probability-based American respondent sample and expert environmental-economist comparison sample

observations.period: Representative U.S. survey and expert comparison

denominator.unit: probability-based American respondents and environmental economists in source-specific samples; exact public-abstract counts not used in the bounded extraction

instrument_preferences.value: respondents preferred weaker environmental targets for consumer taxes and stronger targets for standards

cost_belief.value: unlike expert environmental economists, respondents believed market-based instruments raise consumer energy bills more than standards

policy_tradeoff.value: support for stringency and cost-effectiveness can point in different directions across instruments

observations.method: Survey comparison holding environmental impacts constant across policy instruments, with a separate expert-belief comparison; the source is not treated as a household bill or pollution panel.
observations.uncertainty: Beliefs and preferences do not identify actual pass-through, household energy bills, pollution, health, fairness judgments, or later political action.
observations.subgroup: Probability-based U.S. respondents and environmental economists in separate samples; detailed subgroup results are not extracted here.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may care about fairness, control, enforceability, trust, or distribution in addition to total cost; choosing a standard is not proof of ignorance or irrationality.

denominator.unit: respondents assigned to educational-video and comparison conditions; exact outcome-specific denominator not disclosed in the bounded extraction

belief_change.value: videos explaining pass-through and cost-effectiveness moved respondent beliefs closer to those of experts

information_channel.value: economic understanding can alter how voters evaluate environmental policy instruments

observations.method: Randomized or experimental educational-video exposure within the survey design; the bounded extraction preserves the direction of the reported effects without inventing effect sizes.
observations.uncertainty: A short information treatment may not persist, change actual political behavior, or overcome concerns about fairness, trust, or local incidence.
observations.subgroup: Survey respondents assigned to information and comparison conditions; subgroup durability is not established here.
observations.counterinterpretation: Moving beliefs toward expert estimates does not prove that experts have the correct distributional or ethical judgment for every household or place.

denominator.unit: model-defined policy-choice pathway from beliefs and political constraints to instrument selection

political_constraint.value: political constraints alone can set market-based instruments below the Pigouvian benchmark

instrument_switch.value: imperfect economic literacy can flip a politically constrained planner from a market-based instrument to a less cost-effective standard

actual_outcomes.value: actual household bills, rebates, pollution, health, and later political action are not observed in the bounded route

observations.method: Model of politically constrained policy design informed by the survey evidence; model implications are kept separate from observed policy outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The result depends on model assumptions about beliefs, policy instruments, political constraints, and welfare; it is not a forecast of a particular U.S. policy or environmental result.
observations.subgroup: Model-defined voters and policymakers rather than a linked household panel.
observations.counterinterpretation: A less cost-effective instrument in the model may still be preferred for reasons the model does not fully capture, including transparency, accountability, distribution, or public trust.

related_sources.claim: Official NBER PDF used for the paper's abstract and method context.

boundary: This record shows that cost beliefs differ between representative respondents and environmental economists, that information can move beliefs and policy support, and that a model can translate those beliefs into different policy instruments. It does not show actual household bills, distributional fairness, pollution or health results, durable belief change, or voting.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER working-paper PDF used for the extracted findings; survey data, expert sample, and model replication are not locally reproduced.
